"Pass" is about movement or transfer — something or someone moves from one point, person, place, or state to another. Once you feel this central idea, almost every meaning of the word will make sense naturally.

1. To go by something or someone (physical movement)

You are moving, and something or someone is alongside you — then behind you.

The bus passed me without stopping.
A police car passed at high speed.
She walked past the bakery and didn't even look.

This is perhaps the most literal meaning. You move forward; the other thing stays behind you.

2. To go through or across a place

You travel through a place, but you don't stay there. You just move through it.

We passed through three small towns on the way to Delhi.
The road passes through a thick forest.
The river passes under the old stone bridge.

3. To hand something to someone

You pick something up and give it directly to another person nearby.

Can you pass me the salt, please?
He passed the ball to his teammate.
She passed the envelope to the security guard.

The movement here is short — from your hand to theirs.

4. To transfer something from one person (or thing) to another

This is a broader version of "handing." The thing that moves could be a disease, information, a quality, or even a responsibility.

The virus can be passed from person to person through the air.
Parents pass their genes to their children.
Please pass on this message to your manager.
The tradition was passed from generation to generation.

Here, "pass" often works with on or down — you'll see those as phrasal verbs below.

5. To succeed in an exam, test, or inspection

You meet the required standard. You clear the bar.

I passed my driving test on the first try.
She studied hard and passed all her exams.
The building passed the safety inspection.

The opposite is fail. Note that "pass" here does not mean you did brilliantly — it only means you cleared the minimum standard. You could barely pass, or you could pass with high marks.

6. To officially approve something (a law, a bill, a proposal)

A group of people — a government, a committee, a board — votes and officially accepts something.

The government passed a new law banning single-use plastic.
The Parliament passed the budget after a long debate.
The board passed the proposal unanimously.

7. For time to go by

Time moves forward. This is one of the most frequently used meanings.

Time passes so quickly when you're busy.
Three weeks passed before she called back.
The holidays passed too fast.

You can also use it to mean to spend time doing something:

We passed the evening watching old films.
He passed the long wait by reading a book.

Notice the difference:

  • Time passed. → time went by on its own
  • We passed the time. → we filled the time with an activity

8. To go beyond a number, level, or limit (to exceed)

Something crosses over a threshold — a number, a point, a boundary.

The temperature passed 45°C last summer.
The company's profits passed one billion rupees.
The number of applicants passed ten thousand.

Think of it like crossing a line — the thing that was below the number is now above it.

9. To come to an end (especially something unpleasant)

Something difficult — pain, a storm, a bad phase — goes away by itself over time.

Don't worry, the pain will pass.
The storm will pass by midnight.
This difficult period in your life will pass too.

This is a comforting, hopeful use of the word.

10. To decline something / to choose not to take part

You are offered something, and you choose to say "no, thank you."

I'll pass on the dessert — I'm full.
She was offered the role but decided to pass.

In card games, "I pass" means "I choose not to play this turn."

More casually, someone might just say:

"Want to join us?" — "I'll pass." (= No thanks.)

11. To be accepted or mistaken as something else

Someone or something is believed to be something they are not — either because they look like it or act like it.

His Hindi is so fluent that he could pass as a local.
In dim light, the copy could pass for the original.
She tried to pass herself off as a doctor.

The idea is: the person or thing successfully "goes by" without being identified correctly.

12. To overlook or not react to something

You choose to ignore something — a mistake, a rude comment, a small problem.

I'll let that comment pass this time.
The teacher let the mistake pass without correcting it.
He said something offensive, but she let it pass.

13. To make a remark or give a judgment

You express an opinion — often one that is critical or judgmental.

Don't pass judgment on people you don't know.
She passed a few unkind remarks about his work.
It's not fair to pass comments on someone's appearance.

This is almost always used in negative or cautionary sentences — "don't pass judgment," "he keeps passing comments."

14. Bodily functions (medical and everyday use)

In medical or polite everyday contexts:

The doctor asked whether the patient had passed blood. (excreted blood in urine or stool)
"Pass water" = urinate (formal/medical)
"Pass gas" = release gas from the body (polite/informal)

Phrasal verbs are when "pass" combines with a small word (like on, out, up, away) to create a new, specific meaning.

Pass away

To die. This is a gentle, respectful way to say someone died.

Her grandmother passed away peacefully in her sleep.
He passed away after a long illness.

Pass out

Meaning 1: To faint — to suddenly lose consciousness.

She passed out because of the heat.
He hadn't eaten all day and passed out.

Meaning 2: To distribute something to a group of people.

The teacher passed out the question papers.
Volunteers were passing out food to the crowd.

Pass on

Meaning 1: To give or transmit something to the next person or generation.

Please pass on this message to your team.
Grandparents pass on their values to their grandchildren.
The disease is passed on through physical contact.

Meaning 2: To decline something.

I'll pass on the second helping, thanks.

Meaning 3: (Informal/polite) To die — very similar to "pass away."

He passed on last Tuesday.

Pass up

To miss or refuse an opportunity — usually one that was good and you probably shouldn't have missed.

She passed up a great job offer in London.
Don't pass up this chance — it won't come again.

There's often a hint of regret when "pass up" is used.

Pass over

Meaning 1: To skip someone — especially when they deserved something but were unfairly ignored.

He was passed over for promotion again. (Someone junior got the promotion instead.)
She felt passed over and undervalued at work.

Meaning 2: For something to move across a place (used of clouds, storms, aircraft, etc.).

The storm passed over the coast without causing much damage.

Pass off

Meaning 1: To pretend that something false is real; to present something or someone deceptively.

He tried to pass off a cheap copy as an original.
She passed herself off as an expert, but she wasn't.

Meaning 2: (Of an event) To happen in a particular way — especially smoothly.

The event passed off without any trouble.
The ceremony passed off beautifully.

Pass through

To travel through a place without staying for long.

We were just passing through the city — we didn't stop.
Have you ever passed through Mumbai airport?

Pass around / Pass round

To give something to each person in a group, one by one.

Pass the photos around so everyone can see them.
They passed a petition around the office for people to sign.

Pass down

To give something from an older generation to a younger one — traditions, recipes, stories, objects.

This ring has been passed down through five generations.
Folk songs are passed down orally from parents to children.

Pass by

To go past something or someone without stopping or engaging.

Many people passed by without helping the injured man.
Life seemed to be passing him by. (= He felt like he was missing out on life while it moved on without him.)

Pass the time

To do something to fill time while you are waiting or bored.

We played cards to pass the time.
She read a novel to pass the time on the long train journey.

Pass the buck

To shift the blame or responsibility to someone else instead of accepting it yourself.

Instead of solving the problem, he just passed the buck to his colleague.
Stop passing the buck — this is your responsibility.

Pass muster

To reach an acceptable standard; to be good enough.

Your application doesn't quite pass muster — you need more experience.
The new recruit passed muster during the trial week.

Let something pass

To choose not to react to something negative; to overlook it.

He said something rude, but she decided to let it pass.
I'll let this mistake pass, but don't let it happen again.

Come to pass

(Formal or literary) To happen; to occur — used mostly in old texts, religious writing, or dramatic speech.

And it came to pass that the king fell ill.
Everything she had predicted came to pass.
A Quick Summary of the Core Meanings

To bring it all together, here are the main things "pass" (as a verb) can mean:

  • Move past something → The car passed us.
  • Travel through a place → We passed through Jaipur.
  • Hand something → Pass me the book.
  • Transfer something → The disease passes through water.
  • Succeed in a test → She passed her exams.
  • Approve officially → They passed the new bill.
  • Time goes by → Hours passed.
  • Spend time → We passed the evening talking.
  • Exceed a number → It passed 100 degrees.
  • Come to an end → The pain will pass.
  • Decline something → I'll pass.
  • Be mistaken for something → He passed as a local.
  • Overlook something → Let it pass.
  • Express a judgment → Don't pass judgment.

The word "pass" is deceptively simple — it looks small, but it carries a rich range of meanings, all connected by the idea of movement or transition from one state, place, or person to another. Once you see that thread, the word becomes very intuitive.
